rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Sodium hydroxide** — white, deliquescent, mp 318 °C, strongly exothermic in water — is the strongest cheap base in the lab: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ completely. It **precipitates** metal hydroxides with exam-signature colours: pale blue Cu(OH)₂ (insoluble in excess), dirty green Fe(OH)₂, reddish-brown Fe(OH)₃, and white Zn(OH)₂/Al(OH)₃ that **dissolve in excess** as zincate/aluminate because they are amphoteric; ammonium…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The crust on an old pellet*** — a NaOH pellet left uncapped overnight gains a white crust and then a pool of solution: it drank CO₂ (2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O) and moisture from the air — deliquescence plus carbonation in one bench demonstration.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Base of the Chemical World Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is produced on a scale matched only by sulphuric acid. Its two faces — a **strong base** that neutralises and precipitates, and a **strong alkali** that absorbs acidic gases like CO₂ and SO₂ — plus its manufacture route make this topic a guaranteed short-question source.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Properties - White deliquescent solid, mp 318 °C; extremely soluble in water with strong heat evolution; fully dissociated: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ — a **strong monobasic base**. - Soapy touch, corrosive to skin (saponifies fats) — hence "caustic". - Absorbs CO₂ and moisture from air (must be stoppered): 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Ppt colours: Cu blue, Fe2+ green, Fe3+ brown, Zn/Al/Pb white-soluble-in-excess. CO2: limited Na2CO3, excess NaHCO3. Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2.

rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the action of sodium hydroxide on solutions of copper sulphate, ferric chloride and zinc sulphate, noting the behaviour in excess NaOH.** — **Copper sulphate:** addition of NaOH gives a **pale blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide, CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate does **not** dissolve in…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): What is observed when carbon dioxide is passed through sodium hydroxide solution (i) in limited amount, (ii) in excess?** — **(i) Limited CO₂:** the hydroxide is converted to the carbonate — 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O — no visible change beyond possible slight cloudiness.…

rows.text: When writing precipitation equations, include the observation (colour + "insoluble/soluble in excess") — the observation carries the mark as often as the equation.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Amphoteric hydroxides are the qualitative-analysis switch: Zn(OH)2 dissolving in excess NaOH while Cu(OH)2 sits stubbornly blue is the same acid-base duality that defines the border between the metal and non-metal sides of the periodic table.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: NaOH: white deliquescent solid, mp 318 C, very soluble (exothermic), strong monobasic base, soapy touch, absorbs CO2+H2O from air -> Na2CO3 crust. rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: World production of NaOH is about 80 million tonnes a year, almost all of it co-produced with chlorine — the two are chained together by the brine electrolysis, which is why a paper-making boom raises chlorine prices.

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH but Cu(OH)₂ does not - Zinc and aluminium hydroxides are **amphoteric**: their oxides/hydroxides react with strong alkali to form zincate/aluminate, Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O. Copper(II) hydroxide is purely basic — no acid character — so excess NaOH leaves the pale blue precipitate untouched.…  ·  ## 5. rows.text: Give the electrode reactions of the chlor-alkali process and name the three products.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"Soluble in excess" means the hydroxide is amphoteric:** Zn(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Pb(OH)₂ dissolve in excess NaOH; Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂/₃ do not — memorise which side of the line each cation sits on.  ·  **NaOH does not precipitate NH₃:** ammonium salts give no precipitate with NaOH — only ammonia gas on warming; writing "NH₄OH ppt" is wrong.
